reason: The sources provide over 15 verifiable claims about the coelacanth's discovery, anatomy, and unique biology supported by multiple citations.
story: On December 22, 1938, museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer spotted a strange blue fin in a fisherman's catch in South Africa. She had found a coelacanth, a creature thought to have gone extinct 66 million years ago with the dinosaurs. This 'Lazarus' fish was unlike anything modern science had seen. It lacks a true backbone, possessing instead a pressurized, oil-filled tube called a notochord. It has a hinged skull that allows its mouth to swing open like a trapdoor and a 'rostral organ' in its snout that detects electrical signals from prey. Scientists later discovered that these survivors are more closely related to humans and land animals than to 99% of other fish. They are deep-sea ghosts that live for 100 years, perform vertical headstands in the current, and endure a staggering five-year pregnancy before giving birth to live pups.
angle: Thought extinct for 66 million years, this fish has an oil-filled tube instead of a spine, a hinged skull, and a five-year pregnancy.

claims.claim: The coelacanth was believed to have become extinct approximately 66 million years ago at the end of the Cretaceous period.
The first living specimen was discovered on December 22, 1938, off the coast of South Africa.
Museum curator Marjorie Courtenay-Latimer discovered the fish among a fisherman's catch on a trawler.
Ichthyologist J.L.B. Smith confirmed the discovery and named the species Latimeria chalumnae.
The coelacanth possesses fleshy, lobed fins that resemble limbs and move in a pattern similar to a walking reptile.
The fish has an oil-filled notochord instead of a bony vertebral column or backbone.
The coelacanth has a unique intracranial joint in its skull that allows it to open its mouth extremely wide.
It possesses a rostral organ in its head used for electroreception to detect prey.
Coelacanths have been observed performing 'headstands,' swimming vertically in the water.
The species gives birth to live young, with embryos developing inside the female's body.
Recent research suggests the gestation period for a coelacanth is approximately five years.
Coelacanths are more closely related to tetrapods (land-living vertebrates) than to ray-finned fish.
The fish has a lifespan of approximately 100 years.
The flesh of the coelacanth is oily and unpleasant-tasting, containing compounds that can cause diarrhea.
A second species was discovered in Indonesia in the late 1990s.
The coelacanth's scales are armor-like and secrete a slimy mucus.

disputed: The exact gestation period: S7 cites 14 months while S1 and S5 cite 5 years based on more recent research; the script should attribute the 5-year figure to recent studies.
The closest relative to tetrapods: While all sources agree coelacanths are closely related to tetrapods, S2 and S4 clarify that lungfish are actually the closest living relatives.
